rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: Draw energy band diagrams of n-type and p-type semiconductors at temperature \(T > 0\,\mathrm{K}\), depicting the donor and acceptor energy levels. Mention the significance of these levels.
rows.solution:
**n-type semiconductor.** The band diagram shows the valence band, the conduction band above it separated by the gap \(E_g\), and — the new feature — a **donor level \(E_D\) drawn just below the bottom of the conduction band**, typically about \(0{\cdot}01\) eV below \(E_C\) in germanium and \(0{\cdot}05\) eV in silicon. At \(T > 0\) K the donor level has given up its electrons: the conduction band carries plenty of electrons, while the valence band holds only the few holes left by ordinary thermal excitation across the full gap.

**p-type semiconductor.** Here the extra level is an **acceptor level \(E_A\) drawn just above the top of the valence band**, about \(0{\cdot}01\)–\(0{\cdot}05\) eV above \(E_V\). At \(T > 0\) K electrons have been lifted from the valence band into it, so the valence band carries plenty of holes while the conduction band holds only a few thermally excited electrons.

**Significance of these levels.**

The whole point is the **size of the gap that has to be crossed**. Exciting a carrier across the full band gap \(E_g\) costs about \(1{\cdot}1\) eV in silicon, whereas thermal energy at room temperature is only \(k_BT \approx 0{\cdot}026\) eV — so that process is rare. The donor and acceptor levels sit within a few hundredths of an electron-volt of the nearest band, a gap that thermal energy covers easily.

So at room temperature essentially **every** donor is ionised, and essentially every acceptor has captured an electron. A dopant concentration of even one part per million therefore supplies far more carriers than the intrinsic process does, and the conductivity rises by orders of magnitude. The impurity level is what converts a poor conductor into a useful one, and it is also what makes the carrier type controllable: donors give electrons, acceptors give holes.

rows.stem: Draw the graph showing the variation of the number (N) of scattered alpha particles with scattering angle \((\theta)\) in Geiger – Marsden experiment. Infer two conclusions from the graph.
rows.solution:
**The graph.** Plot the number \(N\) of scattered alpha particles against the scattering angle \(\theta\). The curve begins extremely high at small angles and falls very steeply — over several orders of magnitude, so a logarithmic vertical scale is usual — flattening into a long, almost horizontal tail that stays just above zero all the way out to \(\theta = 180^\circ\). Rutherford's analysis gives \(N \propto \cosec^{4}(\theta/2)\), which is the shape drawn.

**Two conclusions.**

*(i) Most of an atom is empty space.* The overwhelming majority of alpha particles pass through the gold foil almost undeviated, meeting nothing substantial on the way. Only about \(0{\cdot}14\%\) are scattered through more than \(1^\circ\).

*(ii) The positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus.* A small number of particles are deflected through more than \(90^\circ\), and a very few are turned right back along their path. Reversing a fast, massive alpha particle requires a concentrated positive charge heavy enough not to simply recoil away — and the rarity of such events measures how small that target is: about \(10^{-15}\) m against an atomic \(10^{-10}\) m.

It is the *rarity* that carries the information, not the existence of large-angle events. The Thomson model, with positive charge spread through the whole atomic volume, could produce no backscattering at all.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem:
Plot suitable graphs to show the variation of photoelectric current with the collector plate potential for the incident radiation of
(i) the same intensity but different frequencies \(
u_1\), \(
u_2\) and \(
u_3\) \((
u_1 < 
u_2 < 
u_3)\)
(ii) the same frequency but different intensities \(I_1\), \(I_2\) and \(I_3\) \((I_1 < I_2 < I_3)\)
rows.solution:
Both graphs plot photoelectric current on the vertical axis against collector plate potential on the horizontal, with retarding (negative) potential to the left of the origin and accelerating (positive) potential to the right. Each curve rises from zero at its stopping potential, climbs through the origin region, and flattens to a **saturation plateau** at large positive potential.

**(i) Same intensity, different frequencies \(\nu_1 < \nu_2 < \nu_3\).**

Three curves that **share a common saturation plateau** but cut the negative axis at three different points:

\(\left|V_{03}\right| > \left|V_{02}\right| > \left|V_{01}\right|\)

The higher the frequency, the more energetic the fastest photoelectrons, and the larger the retarding potential needed to stop them. But the *number* emitted per second is fixed by how many photons arrive, which is the same for all three — so all three saturate at the same current.

**(ii) Same frequency, different intensities \(I_1 < I_2 < I_3\).**

Three curves that **all meet the negative axis at the same stopping potential \(-V_0\)** but level off at three different plateaus, the saturation current rising in the order \(I_1 < I_2 < I_3\).

Intensity fixes how many photons arrive per second and hence how many electrons are ejected, but not how energetic each one is — so the plateau height scales with intensity while the stopping potential does not move.

The pair of graphs is the whole photoelectric effect in two pictures: **frequency moves the stopping potential and leaves the plateau alone; intensity moves the plateau and leaves the stopping potential alone.** Neither behaviour is explicable on a wave picture, where brighter light should also mean more energetic electrons.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: Write the characteristics of a p-n junction which make it suitable for rectification.
rows.solution:
The characteristic that matters is that a p-n junction conducts in **one direction only**.

Under **forward bias** the applied voltage opposes the barrier potential, narrowing the depletion layer. Once the applied voltage exceeds the threshold — about \(0{\cdot}3\) V for germanium, \(0{\cdot}7\) V for silicon — the current rises very steeply, almost exponentially, and the junction's resistance is low.

Under **reverse bias** the applied voltage adds to the barrier potential, widening the depletion layer. Only a tiny reverse saturation current flows, of the order of microamperes, carried by minority carriers; the resistance is very high, and the current stays almost independent of voltage until breakdown.

**Why this makes it a rectifier.** The junction therefore behaves as a closed switch for one polarity and an open switch for the other. Fed with an alternating voltage, it passes current during the half-cycles that forward-bias it and blocks the half-cycles that reverse-bias it, so the current through a load connected in series is **unidirectional** even though the source alternates. That conversion of alternating to direct current is rectification.

The asymmetry is the entire property: a component with the same resistance either way — a resistor — could never rectify, however large or small that resistance was.

rows.stem: Define the term – Distance of closest approach. How will it be affected, for an \(\alpha\) - particle, if kinetic energy of the particle is doubled ?
rows.solution:
**Definition.** The distance of closest approach is the least distance to which an alpha particle, fired directly at a nucleus, can get before its motion is reversed. Travelling straight at the nucleus it is decelerated by the Coulomb repulsion, and at that distance it comes momentarily to rest, having converted all its kinetic energy into electrostatic potential energy.

**Expression.** Equating the two energies for an alpha particle of charge \(2e\) approaching a nucleus of atomic number \(Z\):

\(K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(2e)(Ze)}{r_0}\)

\(r_0 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2Ze^{2}}{K}\)

**Effect of doubling the kinetic energy.** Everything in that expression except \(K\) is a constant of the particle and the target, so

\(r_0 \propto \dfrac{1}{K}\)

Doubling \(K\) therefore **halves \(r_0\)** — the alpha particle penetrates twice as close to the nucleus before turning back.

The inverse dependence is what made the experiment a probe of nuclear size. Rutherford could shrink \(r_0\) by using faster alpha particles, and as long as his results kept obeying the Coulomb scattering formula, he knew the particle had not yet reached the nucleus. Departures from that formula at high energy would mark the point where \(r_0\) had become comparable to the nuclear radius itself.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A point source in air is kept 24 cm in front of a concave spherical glass surface \(({}_{a}\mu_{g} = 1.5)\) and radius of curvature 60 cm. Find the nature of the image formed and its distance from the point source.
rows.solution:
Refraction at a single spherical surface, with the light going from air into glass.

**Setting up.** Take the direction of the incident light as positive and the pole of the surface as origin. The source is real and 24 cm in front, so \(u = -24\) cm. The surface is **concave** as the light meets it, so its centre of curvature lies on the same side as the object: \(R = -60\) cm. With \(\mu_1 = 1\) in air and \(\mu_2 = 1{\cdot}5\) in glass:

\(\dfrac{\mu_2}{v} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}\)

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} - \dfrac{1}{(-24)} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 - 1}{(-60)}\)

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} + \dfrac{1}{24} = -\dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{60} = -\dfrac{1}{120}\)

\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{120} - \dfrac{5}{120} = -\dfrac{6}{120} = -\dfrac{1}{20}\)

\(v = -30\ \text{cm}\)

**Nature of the image.** The negative sign places the image on the same side of the surface as the object — light does not actually converge there, so the image is **virtual** (and erect).

**Distance from the source.** Both lie on the same side of the surface, the source 24 cm away and the image 30 cm away:

\(\left|v - u\right| = \left|-30 - (-24)\right| = 6\ \text{cm}\)

The image is 6 cm behind the source, i.e. **6 cm farther from the surface than the object is**.

The direction of the shift is what a concave surface should do here: it diverges the light further, so the source appears pushed away rather than drawn nearer. Note that the answer the question asks for is not \(\left|v\right|\) itself — it wants the separation of object and image, so the two distances must be subtracted rather than one of them quoted.

rows.stem:
Calculate the energy released in MeV in the following reaction :
\({}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + \mathrm{n}\)
Given :
\(m\left({}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\right) = 2.014102\) u
\(m\left({}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\right) = 3.016049\) u
\(m\left({}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\right) = 4.002603\) u
\(m_{\mathrm{n}} = 1.008665\) u
rows.solution:
This is the deuterium–tritium fusion reaction:

\({}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + {}^{1}_{0}n\)

Both bookkeeping checks pass: mass number \(2 + 3 = 4 + 1\), charge \(1 + 1 = 2 + 0\).

**Mass defect.**

\(\Delta m = \left[m({}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}) + m({}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H})\right] - \left[m({}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}) + m_n\right]\)

\(\Delta m = (2{\cdot}014102 + 3{\cdot}016049) - (4{\cdot}002603 + 1{\cdot}008665)\)

\(\Delta m = 5{\cdot}030151 - 5{\cdot}011268\)

\(\Delta m = 0{\cdot}018883\ \text{u}\)

**Energy released.**

\(E = \Delta m \times 931{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{MeV} = 0{\cdot}018883 \times 931{\cdot}5\)

\(E = 17{\cdot}59\ \text{MeV}\)

Two things are worth noticing about that number. It is enormous for so few nucleons — about \(3{\cdot}5\) MeV per nucleon, against roughly \(0{\cdot}85\) MeV per nucleon for the fission of uranium — which is why fusion is the more energetic process per unit mass. And the reason is visible on the binding-energy curve: helium-4 is an exceptionally tightly bound nucleus, sitting well above the smooth trend for its mass number, so forming it releases an unusually large amount.

This particular reaction is the one fusion reactors aim at, precisely because it has the largest cross-section at the lowest attainable temperature of any candidate.

rows.stem: Explain with the help of a suitable diagram, the phenomenon on which an optical fibre works. Mention any two uses of optical fibres.
rows.solution:
**The principle: total internal reflection.**

When light travels from a denser medium into a rarer one, it bends *away* from the normal. As the angle of incidence increases, the refracted ray bends further until, at a particular angle called the **critical angle** \(i_c\), it grazes along the surface at \(90^\circ\). Beyond that angle no refraction is possible at all and the light is **reflected entirely** back into the denser medium.

\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{n_{\text{rarer}}}{n_{\text{denser}}}\)

**The diagram.** Draw a boundary between a denser medium below and a rarer one above, with rays leaving a point source in the denser medium at increasing angles. The first, at small incidence, is mostly refracted out with a weak partial reflection. The second, at exactly \(i_c\), emerges grazing along the surface. The third, at \(i > i_c\), has **no refracted ray at all** — it is totally reflected back.

**Applied to a fibre.** An optical fibre is a thin core of high refractive index surrounded by a cladding of lower index. Light entering one end strikes the core–cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected; it strikes the far side, is reflected again, and so travels down the fibre by thousands of successive total internal reflections. Because each reflection is *total*, essentially no energy is lost at the walls — and this continues even when the fibre is bent, so the light follows the curve of the pipe.

**Two uses.**

- **Medical endoscopy** — a bundle of fibres carries an image out from inside the body, letting internal organs be examined without surgery.
- **Optical communication** — signals are sent as light pulses down fibres over long distances, with far greater bandwidth and far lower loss than electrical cables.

(Fibres are also used in decorative lighting and as sensors for pressure and temperature.)

Total internal reflection is what distinguishes a fibre from an ordinary mirror pipe: a metallic reflector loses a few per cent of the light at every bounce, which after a thousand bounces leaves nothing, whereas a totally internally reflecting boundary loses none.

rows.stem:
A parallel beam of light of wavelength 600 nm is incident normally on a slit of width 0.2 mm. If the resulting diffraction pattern is observed on a screen 1 m away, find the distance of
(i) first minimum, and
(ii) second maximum, from the central maximum.
rows.solution:
Single-slit diffraction, with \(\lambda = 600\ \mathrm{nm} = 600 \times 10^{-9}\) m, slit width \(a = 0{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{mm} = 0{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-3}\) m and screen distance \(D = 1\) m. For small angles the distance on the screen is \(y = D\sin\theta\).

**(i) First minimum.**

Minima occur where \(a\sin\theta = n\lambda\); for the first, \(n = 1\):

\(y_1 = \dfrac{\lambda D}{a} = \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1}{0{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-3}} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 3\ \text{mm}\)

**(ii) Second maximum.**

The secondary maxima fall roughly midway between consecutive minima, at

\(a\sin\theta = \left(n + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda\)

The **second** secondary maximum has \(n = 2\), so \(a\sin\theta = \dfrac{5\lambda}{2}\):

\(y = \dfrac{5}{2} \times \dfrac{\lambda D}{a} = \dfrac{5}{2} \times \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1}{0{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{5}{2} \times 3 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(y = 7{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 7{\cdot}5\ \text{mm}\)

The two results sit either side of the pattern's structure: the central bright band runs from \(-3\) mm to \(+3\) mm, so it is 6 mm wide — twice the spacing of every band beyond it. The second secondary maximum at 7·5 mm lies between the second minimum (6 mm) and the third (9 mm), as it should.

Note that the half-integer rule for the secondary maxima is an approximation: the true maxima sit slightly closer to the central peak than the midpoints, because the envelope is falling across each band. At this level the midpoint value is the expected answer.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem:
A thin equiconvex lens of radius of curvature R made of material of refractive index \(\mu_1\) is kept coaxially, in contact with an equiconcave lens of the same radius of curvature and refractive index \(\mu_2\) \((>\mu_1)\).
Find :
(i) the ratio of their powers, and
(ii) the power of the combination and its nature.
rows.solution:
Both lenses have the same radius of curvature \(R\), so the geometry is common to them and only the refractive indices and the signs differ.

**(i) Ratio of the powers.**

For the **equiconvex** lens of index \(\mu_1\), the two surfaces have \(R_1 = +R\) and \(R_2 = -R\):

\(P_1 = (\mu_1 - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{-R}\right) = (\mu_1 - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}\)

For the **equiconcave** lens of index \(\mu_2\), the signs reverse: \(R_1 = -R\) and \(R_2 = +R\):

\(P_2 = (\mu_2 - 1)\left(-\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R}\right) = -(\mu_2 - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}\)

Dividing, the common factor \(2/R\) cancels:

\(\dfrac{P_1}{P_2} = \dfrac{(\mu_1 - 1)}{-(\mu_2 - 1)} = \dfrac{(\mu_1 - 1)}{(1 - \mu_2)}\)

The ratio is negative, as it must be — one lens converges and the other diverges.

**(ii) Power of the combination, and its nature.**

For thin lenses in contact the powers add:

\(P = P_1 + P_2 = (\mu_1 - 1)\dfrac{2}{R} - (\mu_2 - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}\)

\(P = \dfrac{2}{R}\left[(\mu_1 - 1) - (\mu_2 - 1)\right]\)

\(P = \dfrac{2(\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{R}\)

Since the question states \(\mu_2 > \mu_1\), the bracket is negative and so is \(P\). **The combination is diverging.**

The two \(-1\) terms cancel exactly, which is the tidy feature of this pair: the combined power depends only on the *difference* of the indices, not on either value separately. Had the two lenses been made of the same glass, \(\mu_1 = \mu_2\), the power would be exactly zero — the pair would form a parallel-sided block of glass and behave as no lens at all.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem:
Photoelectrons are emitted from a metal surface when illuminated with UV light of wavelength 330 nm. The minimum amount of energy required to emit the electrons from the surface is \(3.5 \times 10^{-19}\) J. Calculate :
(i) the energy of the incident radiation, and
(ii) the kinetic energy of the photoelectron.
rows.solution:
**(i) Energy of the incident radiation.**

\(E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{330 \times 10^{-9}}\)

\(E = \dfrac{1{\cdot}989 \times 10^{-25}}{3{\cdot}3 \times 10^{-7}} = 6{\cdot}027 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\)

In electron-volts, \(E = \dfrac{6{\cdot}027 \times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 3{\cdot}77\ \text{eV}\).

**(ii) Kinetic energy of the photoelectron.**

"The minimum amount of energy required to emit the electrons from the surface" is the **work function** \(\phi_0 = 3{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-19}\) J. Einstein's photoelectric equation gives the maximum kinetic energy as what is left of the photon's energy after that cost is paid:

\(K_{\max} = E - \phi_0 = 6{\cdot}027 \times 10^{-19} - 3{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-19}\)

\(K_{\max} = 2{\cdot}527 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\)

or about \(1{\cdot}58\) eV.

Two points about the structure of the answer. The photon energy exceeds the work function, so emission does occur — had it not, no electron would be freed however intense the light. And this is the energy of the *fastest* electrons only: those freed from deeper in the metal lose some energy on the way out and emerge with less, so the emitted electrons have kinetic energies spread all the way from zero up to this maximum. The corresponding threshold wavelength for this metal is \(hc/\phi_0 \approx 568\) nm, in the visible range.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: State the working principle of an LED. Write any two important advantages and two disadvantages of LED.
rows.solution:
**Working principle.**

A light-emitting diode is a heavily doped p-n junction operated under **forward bias**. When forward biased, electrons are driven from the n-region across the junction into the p-region, and holes from the p-region into the n-region. Near the junction the concentration of these injected minority carriers rises well above equilibrium, and they **recombine** with the majority carriers already there.

Each recombination annihilates an electron–hole pair, and the energy released — close to the band gap \(E_g\) — is emitted as a **photon**:

\(h\nu \approx E_g\)

The colour of the light is therefore fixed by the band gap of the semiconductor used, which is why LEDs are made from compound semiconductors such as GaAs, GaAsP and GaN rather than from silicon: silicon's recombination releases its energy as lattice vibrations, not light.

**Two advantages.**

- **Low operating voltage and very low power consumption** — an LED runs on a volt or two and a few milliamperes.
- **Long life and ruggedness**, with no filament to burn out and no fragile glass envelope.

(They also switch extremely fast, in nanoseconds, which is what makes them usable as optical transmitters.)

**Two disadvantages.**

- **The light output is restricted to a narrow band of wavelengths** set by the band gap, so a single LED cannot produce white light directly.
- **They are easily damaged by excess voltage or current**, and by the overheating that follows, so a series current-limiting resistor is essential.

(Cost per unit of light output has historically been higher than for conventional lamps, though this has fallen sharply.)

rows.stem:
(i) Monochromatic light is incident on a surface separating two media. The frequency of the light after refraction remains unaffected but its wavelength changes. Why ?
(ii) The frequency of an electromagnetic radiation is \(1.0 \times 10^{11}\) Hz. Identify the radiation and mention its two uses.
rows.solution:
**(i) Why frequency is unchanged but wavelength is not.**

Refraction is the interaction of the incident light with the atoms of the medium. The atoms behave as oscillators that are **driven** by the incoming electromagnetic wave, and a driven oscillator responds at the frequency of whatever drives it — not at a frequency of its own choosing. The light re-radiated by these forced oscillations therefore carries the **same frequency** as the incident light.

Frequency is a property of the **source**, and nothing at a boundary can change it. If it could, wave crests would have to accumulate at or disappear from the interface, which is impossible for a continuous wave.

What does change is the **speed**. In a medium of refractive index \(\mu\),

\(v = \dfrac{c}{\mu}\)

and since \(v = \nu\lambda\) with \(\nu\) fixed, the wavelength must change in step:

\(\lambda_m = \dfrac{v}{\nu} = \dfrac{c}{\mu\nu} = \dfrac{\lambda_0}{\mu}\)

So the wavelength shortens by the factor \(\mu\) on entering a denser medium.

**(ii) Identifying radiation of frequency \(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{11}\) Hz.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{c}{\nu} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{11}} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 3\ \text{mm}\)

A wavelength of 3 mm (100 GHz) lies in the **microwave** region, at its short-wavelength end where it borders the far infrared.

**Two uses of microwaves:**

- **RADAR** — for aircraft navigation and speed measurement, microwaves being short enough to be beamed narrowly yet long enough to penetrate cloud.
- **Microwave ovens** — the frequency is chosen to be absorbed by water molecules, heating food from within.

(They also carry satellite and mobile-telephone communications.)

The boundaries between the named bands are conventions rather than physical divisions, and the marking scheme accordingly accepts the neighbouring names as well.

rows.stem:
(i) Trace the path of a ray of light PQ which is incident at an angle i on one face of a glass prism of angle A. It then emerges out from the other face at an angle e. Use the ray diagram to prove that the angle through which the ray is deviated is given by \(\angle\delta = \angle i + \angle e - \angle A\).
(ii) What will be the minimum value of \(\delta\) if the ray passes symmetrically through the prism ?
rows.solution:
**(i) Path of the ray and the deviation formula.**

*The diagram.* A ray PQ strikes face AB of a prism of refracting angle A at an angle of incidence \(i\). It refracts into the prism at angle \(r_1\), travels to face AC, meets it at angle \(r_2\), and emerges at angle \(e\) along RS. Extending the incident ray forward and the emergent ray backward, they meet at an angle \(\delta\) — the total deviation.

*The deviation at each surface.* At each face the ray is turned through the difference between the angles on either side of the normal, and the two turnings add:

\(\delta = (i - r_1) + (e - r_2) = (i + e) - (r_1 + r_2)\)

*Relating \(r_1 + r_2\) to A.* Let the normals at Q and R meet at O. In the quadrilateral AQOR the angles at Q and R are both \(90^\circ\), so the other two are supplementary:

\(\angle A + \angle QOR = 180^\circ \qquad \text{...(1)}\)

In the triangle QOR:

\(\angle QOR + r_1 + r_2 = 180^\circ \qquad \text{...(2)}\)

Comparing (1) and (2):

\(r_1 + r_2 = A\)

*Substituting:*

\(\delta = i + e - A\)

which is the required relation.

**(ii) Minimum deviation for symmetric passage.**

The deviation is not monotonic in \(i\): as \(i\) increases from a small value, \(\delta\) first falls, reaches a single minimum, and then rises again. Every value of \(\delta\) above the minimum is produced at *two* different angles of incidence, and by the reversibility of light those two are \(i\) and \(e\) interchanged. The minimum is the one place where the two coincide.

The ray therefore passes **symmetrically** through the prism at minimum deviation, travelling parallel to the base, with

\(i = e \qquad\text{and}\qquad r_1 = r_2 = \dfrac{A}{2}\)

Putting \(e = i\) into the deviation formula gives the minimum value:

\(\delta_{\min} = 2i - A\)

Equivalently, in terms of the prism's refractive index, \(\mu = \dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_{\min}}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}\) — the relation on which the standard measurement of \(\mu\) by a spectrometer rests, and the reason minimum deviation is the configuration worth singling out.

rows.stem:
Consider the following waves :
(i) \(y_1 = a \sin \omega t\)
(ii) \(y_2 = a \sin 2\omega t\)
(iii) \(y_3 = a \sin (2\omega t + \phi)\)
(iv) \(y_4 = a \sin \left(4\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)
Which pair of the waves coming from two sources \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) will produce interference ?
rows.context: The principle of superposition is used to understand the phenomenon of interference of light waves. The principle states that at a particular point, the resultant displacement produced by a number of waves is the vector sum of the displacements produced by each wave. Light waves from two coherent sources produce interference pattern. Thomas Young devised a way to obtain two coherent sources using two identical pinholes (\(S_1\) and \(S_2\)) illuminated by a single monochromatic pinhole source S. Using these sources in his experiment known as Young's double slit experiment, Young studied the interference pattern. The pattern consists of alternate bright and dark fringes. The distance between two successive bright or dark finges depends on the distance between \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), the distance of the screen from the plane of \(S_1S_2\) and the wavelength of light used.
rows.solution:
Sustained interference requires the two superposing waves to have the **same frequency** and a **constant phase difference**. Comparing the four:

- \(y_1 = a\sin\omega t\) — angular frequency \(\omega\)
- \(y_2 = a\sin 2\omega t\) — angular frequency \(2\omega\)
- \(y_3 = a\sin(2\omega t + \phi)\) — angular frequency \(2\omega\)
- \(y_4 = a\sin\left(4\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) — angular frequency \(4\omega\)

Only \(y_2\) and \(y_3\) share a frequency, and their phase difference is the constant \(\phi\). That pair is option (B).

The reason a frequency mismatch rules interference out is that the phase difference between two waves of different frequency grows steadily with time. The pattern it would produce sweeps through every value of the phase difference faster than any detector can follow, so the observed intensity is just the time average — the plain sum of the two intensities, with no maxima or minima anywhere. That is exactly why two independent lamps never produce interference fringes.

rows.stem: Two light waves of the same intensity \(I_0\) each, having a path difference of \(\lambda/4\), emanating from two coherent sources, meet at a point. The resultant intensity at the point will be
rows.context: The principle of superposition is used to understand the phenomenon of interference of light waves. The principle states that at a particular point, the resultant displacement produced by a number of waves is the vector sum of the displacements produced by each wave. Light waves from two coherent sources produce interference pattern. Thomas Young devised a way to obtain two coherent sources using two identical pinholes (\(S_1\) and \(S_2\)) illuminated by a single monochromatic pinhole source S. Using these sources in his experiment known as Young's double slit experiment, Young studied the interference pattern. The pattern consists of alternate bright and dark fringes. The distance between two successive bright or dark finges depends on the distance between \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), the distance of the screen from the plane of \(S_1S_2\) and the wavelength of light used.
rows.solution:
Convert the path difference into a phase difference, then use the two-source formula.

\(\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \Delta x = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)

For two sources of equal intensity \(I_0\) each:

\(I = 4I_0\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2} = 4I_0\cos^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 4I_0\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2} = 4I_0 \times \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(I = 2I_0\)

The answer is (C).

A quarter-wave path difference is the quadrature point, and \(2I_0\) is exactly the intensity the two sources would give if they simply added without interfering — it is the *average* of the pattern. That makes sense: a phase difference of \(\pi/2\) sits precisely halfway between full constructive (\(4I_0\)) and full destructive (\(0\)) interference, and \(\cos^{2}\) is symmetric about that midpoint.

rows.stem: Vandana performs Young's double slit experiment by using orange, green and red lights successively. If the fringe widths measured in the three cases are \(\omega_1\), \(\omega_2\) and \(\omega_3\) respectively, then which of the following is correct ?
rows.context: The principle of superposition is used to understand the phenomenon of interference of light waves. The principle states that at a particular point, the resultant displacement produced by a number of waves is the vector sum of the displacements produced by each wave. Light waves from two coherent sources produce interference pattern. Thomas Young devised a way to obtain two coherent sources using two identical pinholes (\(S_1\) and \(S_2\)) illuminated by a single monochromatic pinhole source S. Using these sources in his experiment known as Young's double slit experiment, Young studied the interference pattern. The pattern consists of alternate bright and dark fringes. The distance between two successive bright or dark finges depends on the distance between \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), the distance of the screen from the plane of \(S_1S_2\) and the wavelength of light used.
rows.solution:
Fringe width in Young's experiment is

\(\omega = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\)

With the same apparatus used for all three colours, \(D\) and \(d\) are fixed, so \(\omega \propto \lambda\) and the ordering of the fringe widths is simply the ordering of the wavelengths.

In the visible spectrum, red has the longest wavelength (about 700 nm), orange is next (about 600 nm) and green the shortest of the three (about 550 nm):

\(\lambda_{\text{red}} > \lambda_{\text{orange}} > \lambda_{\text{green}}\)

Since \(\omega_1\) is orange, \(\omega_2\) green and \(\omega_3\) red:

\(\omega_3 > \omega_1 > \omega_2\)

The answer is (D).

The subscripts are the trap: they follow the order the colours are named in the question, not the order of wavelength, so the answer has to be assembled by matching each subscript to its colour. Physically, longer wavelengths spread the pattern out — which is why a white-light fringe pattern shows red on the outer edge of each coloured band and violet on the inner.

rows.stem: In a Young's double slit experiment, the slit separation is 0.8 mm and the interference pattern is obtained on a screen kept 50 cm from the plane of the slits \(S_1\) and \(S_2\). If the first bright fringe is formed 0.4 mm from the central maximum, the wavelength of light used is
rows.context: The principle of superposition is used to understand the phenomenon of interference of light waves. The principle states that at a particular point, the resultant displacement produced by a number of waves is the vector sum of the displacements produced by each wave. Light waves from two coherent sources produce interference pattern. Thomas Young devised a way to obtain two coherent sources using two identical pinholes (\(S_1\) and \(S_2\)) illuminated by a single monochromatic pinhole source S. Using these sources in his experiment known as Young's double slit experiment, Young studied the interference pattern. The pattern consists of alternate bright and dark fringes. The distance between two successive bright or dark finges depends on the distance between \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), the distance of the screen from the plane of \(S_1S_2\) and the wavelength of light used.
rows.solution:
The \(n^{\text{th}}\) bright fringe sits at

\(y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)

For the first bright fringe, \(n = 1\), so

\(\lambda = \dfrac{y_1 d}{D}\)

Substituting \(y_1 = 0{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{mm} = 0{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-3}\) m, \(d = 0{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{mm} = 0{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-3}\) m and \(D = 50\ \mathrm{cm} = 0{\cdot}5\) m:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{(0{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-3})(0{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-3})}{0{\cdot}5} = \dfrac{3{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-7}}{0{\cdot}5}\)

\(\lambda = 6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} = 640\ \text{nm}\)

The answer is (C).

All three lengths must be in metres before substituting — two of them are given in millimetres and one in centimetres, which is where the arithmetic usually goes wrong. The result, 640 nm, falls in the red part of the visible spectrum, a plausible check that no factor of ten has been lost.

rows.stem:
Consider the effect on the angular separation of the fringes in a Young's double slit experiment due to the following operations :
(i) the screen is moved away from the plane of the slits,
(ii) the separation between the two slits is increased till fringes are observed.
Which of the following options is correct ?
rows.context: The principle of superposition is used to understand the phenomenon of interference of light waves. The principle states that at a particular point, the resultant displacement produced by a number of waves is the vector sum of the displacements produced by each wave. Light waves from two coherent sources produce interference pattern. Thomas Young devised a way to obtain two coherent sources using two identical pinholes (\(S_1\) and \(S_2\)) illuminated by a single monochromatic pinhole source S. Using these sources in his experiment known as Young's double slit experiment, Young studied the interference pattern. The pattern consists of alternate bright and dark fringes. The distance between two successive bright or dark finges depends on the distance between \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), the distance of the screen from the plane of \(S_1S_2\) and the wavelength of light used.

options.label: A
options.text: It remains constant in both cases.

options.label: C
options.text: It remains constant in (i) but decreases in (ii).

options.label: D
options.text: It decreases in (i) but remains constant in (ii).

rows.solution:
The question is about **angular** separation, not the separation measured on the screen, and the two behave differently.

The angular position of the \(n^{\text{th}}\) bright fringe is \(\theta_n = \dfrac{n\lambda}{d}\), so the angular separation between adjacent fringes is

\(\Delta\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d}\)

**The screen distance \(D\) does not appear in it.**

**(i) Moving the screen away.** The angular separation \(\lambda/d\) contains no \(D\), so it **remains constant**. What does change is the linear fringe width \(\omega = \lambda D/d\), which grows in proportion to \(D\) — the pattern is projected larger, but each fringe still subtends the same angle at the slits.

**(ii) Increasing the slit separation \(d\).** Now \(\Delta\theta = \lambda/d\) **decreases**, in inverse proportion. The fringes crowd together both in angle and on the screen.

So it remains constant in (i) but decreases in (ii) — option (C).

The distinction is the substance of the question. The double slit produces a fixed pattern of directions, fully determined by \(\lambda\) and \(d\); the screen merely intercepts that pattern, and moving it back magnifies what is already there without altering it. Only changing \(\lambda\) or \(d\) changes the pattern itself.
